name: Engineering leaders on hiring and training juniors
citation: (1) IBM. Preston Fore, 'IBM is tripling the number of Gen Z entry-level jobs after finding the limits of AI adoption', Fortune, 13 February 2026, https://fortune.com/2026/02/13/tech-giant-ibm-tripling-gen-z-entry-level-hiring-according-to-chro-rewriting-jobs-ai-era/ . source_tier: Mixed. IBM: press (Fortune) reporting remarks made on a conference stage, plus the conference host's own write-up (Charter, trade press). No IBM press release or filing was found. AWS: a YouTube interview (the primary source, a creator channel), then press (The Register, WIRED, Fortune) and a newsletter interview (Platformer). Beane: a trade book from a commercial publisher, resting on one peer-reviewed ethnography (Administrative Science Quarterly, 2019 issue) and on unpublished pooled fieldwork from other researchers. None of the three is a study of software engineers.
access_status: Fortune IBM article: fully read. Charter article of 11 February 2026: fully read (it is short). Charter takeaways piece: the free portion read, the rest is behind the Charter Pro wall. Bloomberg's original IBM report: not opened (paywalled). Axios 13 February 2026: search snippet only (blocked). Berman YouTube video: the auto-generated English captions were downloaded and read around the remark (about 10:30 to 14:30); the audio itself was not listened to. The Register, WIRED, Platformer, Fortune Garman piece: fully read. Beane, The Skill Code: the book text was NOT opened. Read instead: the HarperCollins publisher description, the full TED talk transcript, the Crossref abstract of the ASQ paper, the free opening of the HBR article (the rest is paywalled) and the MIT Sloan write-up of a Beane talk.
author_credentials: Nickle LaMoreaux: chief human resources officer, IBM. She speaks for an employer with an interest in looking like a good place for graduates to work, and the remark was made a few months after IBM announced job cuts. Arvind Krishna: IBM chief executive. Matt Garman: chief executive of Amazon Web Services; joined Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005 (Platformer). He has a direct commercial interest: the remark was made while promoting Kiro, AWS's AI coding tool, which he says can 'guide more junior developers', and AWS sells AI agents to employers. Matt Beane: assistant professor of technology management, University of California, Santa Barbara; research affiliate or Digital Fellow at MIT's Initiative on the Digital Economy; MIT Sloan SM 2014, PhD 2017. Commercial interest: he sells the book and, per MIT Sloan (November 2024), is chief executive and co-founder of SkillBench, a startup selling skill-development insight to companies. Reporters: Preston Fore and Sasha Rogelberg (Fortune), Jena McGregor (Charter managing editor, who also moderated the LaMoreaux session), Simon Sharwood (The Register), Katie Drummond (WIRED), Casey Newton (Platformer; he discloses that his fiance works at Anthropic).

"Build the business case now; even though it may not seem so obvious to your leaders, because AI is going to make your job easier three years from now."

AWS, Berman video, auto-captions at about 11:49 to 11:58 and 12:36 to 12:52, the Kiro framing either side of the remark: "one of the cool things about that is that you can actually guide more junior developers as to like what are great coding practices" ... AWS, The Register 21 Aug 2025 (its cleaned-up version of the same passage): "How's that going to work when ten years in the future you have no one that has learned anything" ... AWS, WIRED 16 Dec 2025 (Garman, Q and A): "That point, by the way, was specifically about software developers, but I think it applies to lots."

AWS, WIRED 16 Dec 2025 (Garman): "You've gotta think longer term about the health of a company, and just saying “OK great, we're never going to hire junior people anymore,” that's just a nonstarter for anyone who's trying to build a long-term company."
AWS, Platformer 23 Jun 2026 (Garman): "This is the reason we're hiring 11,000 interns and new college grads this year at Amazon. They come in with an energy and excitement, a new view on things."
AWS, Platformer 23 Jun 2026 (Garman): "I actually think one of the things we start to look for in employees is not what skill set you have, but whether you have the ability to learn."

AWS, Platformer 23 Jun 2026 (Casey Newton's counterpoint): "The company has cut roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since last October. Its CEO, Andy Jassy, has written that AI will "reduce our total corporate workforce" in the years ahead."

Beane, HarperCollins publisher description of The Skill Code (publisher copy, not the book's text): "decades of research show that you achieved mastery by working with someone who knew more than you did."

Beane, HarperCollins publisher description: "In our grail-like quest to optimize productivity with intelligent technologies like AI and robots, we are separating junior workers from experts in workplaces around the world. It's a looming multi-trillion-dollar problem that few are addressing, until now."
Beane, HarperCollins publisher description: "the three C's—challenge, complexity, and connection—are the basic components of how we develop our most valuable skills."
Beane, TED talk transcript, November 2018: "Right now, we're handling AI in a way that blocks that path. We're sacrificing learning in our quest for productivity."

Beane, TED talk transcript, November 2018: "Organizations were trying harder and harder to get results from AI, and they were peeling learners away from expert work as they did it." ... "Junior bankers were getting cut out of complex analysis"

Beane, TED talk transcript, November 2018 (on residents in robotic surgery): "They got to “see one” plenty, but the “do one” was barely available. So they couldn't struggle, and they weren't learning."
Beane, TED talk transcript, November 2018 (his prescription): "Let's build this combination of struggle and expert support into each AI implementation."

Beane, quoted by MIT Sloan, 12 Nov 2024, from an October 2024 alumni talk: "If you ask an expert to identify the right time to bring a truly optional novice into their work, somebody who by definition will make mistakes and be slower, the practical answer is likely never."

Beane, quoted by MIT Sloan, 12 Nov 2024 (defining challenge): "Working close to the edge of your capability on a certain task. It's close to where you are not performing at your best; you are focused and uncomfortable"
Beane, quoted by MIT Sloan, 12 Nov 2024 (on default chatbots): "it will subtly deprive you of challenge, complexity, and connection the more you use it."

Beane, ASQ 2019 abstract (Crossref): "the radically different practice of robotic surgery greatly limited trainees' role in the work, making approved methods ineffective." ... shadow learning practices "allowed only a minority of robotic surgical trainees to come to competence."
key_claims: IBM (LaMoreaux, 10 February 2026): IBM is tripling entry-level hiring, including software developers and other jobs said to be doable by AI.
IBM: the firms that will be most successful in three to five years are those that keep hiring at entry level now. This is a prediction, offered without data.

IBM: the jobs are not the old jobs. Entry-level roles have been rewritten. Junior developers still code (with AI) and test, but spend more time with marketing teams and clients and on new products. LaMoreaux says HR must 'rewrite every job' (Charter).
IBM (as paraphrased by Fortune): cutting juniors risks a later shortage of mid-level managers, and buying talent from competitors costs more and takes longer to bed in.

AWS (Garman, August 2025): leaders at a leadership group told him AI could replace all their junior people; he called that one of the dumbest things he had heard. His reasons: juniors are the cheapest employees, they are the keenest users of AI tools, and in ten years a firm that stops hiring them has nobody who has learned anything.

AWS (Garman, August 2025): keep hiring graduates and teach them to build software and decompose problems 'just as much as you ever have'. He presents AWS's Kiro tool as part of how that teaching happens.

AWS (Garman, WIRED, December 2025): the remark was specifically about software developers but he thinks it applies widely; a firm with no talent pipeline 'explodes on itself'; never hiring juniors is a 'nonstarter' for a long-term company.
AWS (Garman, Platformer, June 2026): Amazon is hiring 11,000 interns and new college graduates in 2026, and looks for ability to learn over a fixed skill set.

Beane: skill is built on the job by working alongside someone more expert, not mainly in formal training. Intelligent technologies let one expert do the work alone, so the novice becomes optional and is cut out.
Beane: healthy skill development needs three things, challenge, complexity and connection, and default use of AI and robotics erodes all three.
Beane: in robotic surgery, approved training methods failed and only a minority of trainees reached competence, by rule-bending 'shadow learning' (ASQ paper).
Beane: the fix is to design work so novices still struggle near the edge of their ability with an expert close by, and to build AI that coaches rather than replaces that.
headline_figures: IBM: 'tripling our entry-level hiring' (LaMoreaux, 10 February 2026, reported by Charter 11 February and Fortune 13 February 2026). No base number, no target number and no geography are given in Fortune or Charter. Secondary reports (not opened in full) say the tripling is for the US and for 2026 and that IBM declined to give figures.
IBM: 'three to five years from now' is the horizon for LaMoreaux's prediction about which companies will be most successful.
IBM: Fortune describes IBM as a '$240 billion tech giant' (market value, February 2026).
Fortune context: 'The unemployment rate among young college grads sits at 5.6%, hovering near its highest level in more than a decade outside the pandemic.' No source or date is given in the article.

Fortune context: 'A report from Korn Ferry found that 37% of organizations plan to replace early career roles with AI.' The Korn Ferry report itself was not found on the page opened, so the wording and sample are unverified.
Fortune context: Dropbox 'is set to expand its internship and new graduate programs by 25%' (attributed to Bloomberg).

IBM layoffs: Fortune says the cuts announced a week after Krishna's October 2025 comments 'would impact a relatively low single-digit percentage of the company's global workforce' and, with new hiring, 'leave IBM's U.S. headcount roughly flat'.
AWS: '10 years in the future' is Garman's horizon in the August 2025 remark.
AWS: 'over 80 percent of AWS's developers use AI in some way' (The Register's report of Garman, August 2025).
AWS: 'hiring 11,000 interns and new college grads this year at Amazon' (Garman, Platformer, 23 June 2026; 'this year' is 2026).
Amazon counterweight: 'cut roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since last October' (Platformer, June 2026); Fortune reports 14,000 jobs announced in October 2025, 'mostly middle management positions'.
Beane: 'a looming multi-trillion-dollar problem' (publisher copy, no derivation shown).

Beane: ASQ study covered 'a two-year, five-sited, comparative ethnographic study' and 'a blinded interview-based study of surgical learning practices at 13 top-tier teaching hospitals around the U.S.' In the TED talk he says 'I covered 18 of the top US teaching hospitals' (5 plus 13).
Beane: a resident in robotic surgery will 'be lucky if she operates more than 15 minutes during a four-hour procedure' (TED talk, illustrative, not a measured average).
sample_and_method: None of the IBM or AWS material is a study. LaMoreaux's remarks are an executive's statement of hiring intent and a forecast, made in a moderated conference session. Garman's remark is an anecdote (what unnamed leaders at an unnamed 'leadership group' told him) followed by opinion. The supporting numbers (80 percent of AWS developers using AI, 11,000 interns and graduates) are company statements without method. Beane is the only one with research behind him: a two-year comparative ethnography across five hospital sites of robotic and traditional surgery plus blinded interviews about surgical learning at 13 top-tier US teaching hospitals (ASQ, published online January 2018). For the wider claim he pooled field data from other researchers' ethnographies in start-ups, policing, investment banking and online education (TED talk). The book adds settings such as warehouses and bomb disposal (publisher copy and MIT Sloan). All of this is observational and qualitative. There is no randomised or quantitative comparison and no sample of software engineers in the material opened.
evidence_offered: IBM: none beyond the statement. No headcount, no retention or promotion data, no evidence that the rewritten roles produce better engineers. AWS: Garman's own reasoning (cost, AI fluency, pipeline) and Amazon's stated hiring number. Beane: long fieldwork in surgery, and a pattern he reports seeing across other people's field studies. The three C's framework is his synthesis of that fieldwork and was not tested as an intervention in anything opened here.
data_vintage: IBM remarks: 10 February 2026 (Charter summit, New York); Charter article 11 February 2026; Fortune 13 February 2026, 11:43 ET. Krishna's CNN comment: October 2025. Garman remark: video published 18 August 2025 (YouTube metadata, US Pacific time); The Register 21 August 2025; WIRED 16 December 2025; Platformer 23 June 2026 (page metadata gives 24 June 2026 UTC). The Fortune Garman article now carries the date 28 June 2026 and a note that 'A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Dec. 16, 2025', so its text has changed since first publication. Beane: fieldwork from roughly 2013 to 2016; ASQ paper online 9 January 2018 and in the March 2019 issue; TED talk November 2018; HBR September-October 2019; book on sale 11 June 2024. Beane's core evidence predates generative AI coding tools.
figure_provenance: IBM tripling: the origin is LaMoreaux on stage at Charter's Leading with AI Summit on 10 February 2026. Charter's own article (11 February) is the closest thing to a primary record. Bloomberg is credited elsewhere with first reporting it; Fortune (13 February) says only that she 'said this week' and does not name the event. Two versions of the key quote circulate: Charter has 'I think the companies ... are those companies that double down on entry-level hiring in this environment'; Fortune has 'The companies ... that doubled down'. Charter and Fortune also word the tripling line differently ('Yes, that is for software developers, and yes, it's for all these jobs that we're being told AI can do' against 'We are tripling our entry-level hiring, and yes, that is for software developers and all these jobs we're being told AI can do'). No video or transcript was opened to settle which is exact. Garman: the origin is the Matthew Berman YouTube interview. YouTube's metadata dates it 18 August 2025; Gigazine gives 19 August, which is the same upload in Japan time. The interview was not on WIRED or at a conference. Three wordings circulate: 'the dumbest thing I've ever heard' (The Register, TechRadar, most headlines), 'one of the dumbest things I've ever heard' (Fortune, Platformer, and WIRED's 'one of the dumbest ideas'), and 'the stupidest thing' (Gigazine, a back-translation from Japanese). The auto-captions read 'that's the like one the dumbest thing I've ever heard', which fits 'one of the dumbest' better than the headline version, but captions are machine-made. 'Explodes on itself' and 'nonstarter' are from the WIRED interview of December 2025, a separate conversation; do not attribute them to the Berman video. The 11,000 figure is from Platformer, June 2026. Beane: 'cut out' and 'peeling learners away from expert work' are from his 2018 TED talk; 'separating junior workers from experts' is HarperCollins's description of the book. The phrase 'novice optional' is attributed to him by secondary sources and was not seen in a primary text.
population_and_transfer: IBM and AWS statements are about entry-level hires at two very large technology employers and do refer to software developers directly, so they are on topic, but they are statements of intent and not evidence of outcomes. IBM's 'entry-level' is reported elsewhere to include career changers and returners, not only graduates [uncertain]. Beane studied surgical residents, with other settings (junior bankers, police, start-up staff, warehouse workers, bomb technicians) added from pooled fieldwork. Nothing opened here shows him studying software engineers. The mechanism (an expert with a powerful tool no longer needs the novice's hands) transfers to senior engineers with AI coding agents by analogy only.
outcome_measured: IBM and AWS: none. Stated hiring intentions and opinion, not employment data, task performance or retention. Beane: qualitative judgments of whether trainees reached competence and how much hands-on time they got, from observation and interviews. No test scores, no delayed retention measure, no measured on-the-job performance.
limitations_stated: IBM: LaMoreaux concedes the old junior work is automatable. Fortune: 'she admitted that many of the responsibilities that previously defined entry-level jobs can now be automated'. So the commitment is to hire into different jobs, not to keep the old apprenticeship.

IBM: LaMoreaux frames the case as something HR has to argue for against the instincts of business leaders ('even though it may not seem so obvious to your leaders'), which concedes that the short-term numbers point the other way.
IBM: Fortune notes the layoffs announced a week after Krishna's October 2025 remarks, and that US headcount would be 'roughly flat'.
AWS: Garman, asked how AWS measures success with AI in engineering, says in the Berman interview 'I won't pretend that we have kind of that magic measure today' (auto-captions, about 14:15).
AWS: Garman in WIRED: 'One of the things that I tell our own employees is "Your job is going to change." There's no two ways about it.'
AWS: Garman accepts in Platformer that 'half of white-collar jobs may change', and Newton notes his optimism 'doesn't always seem to square with Amazon's own moves'.

Beane: the ASQ abstract limits the finding to surgical trainees in robotic and open surgery. The generalisation to other industries in the TED talk rests on other researchers' data that he pooled, described only in outline.
Beane: he says the minority who did learn got there by breaking rules, which he calls 'not OK' and 'not sustainable' (TED talk), so the study describes a failure, not a tested remedy.
counter_evidence: IBM's announcement sits beside its own cuts: Fortune reports thousands of jobs cut in late 2025 with US headcount roughly flat, so tripling a small undisclosed base may not mean many more juniors. Fortune also cites a Korn Ferry figure that 37% of organisations plan to replace early career roles with AI, and names Dario Amodei and Jim Farley as executives predicting entry-level losses. Amazon has cut roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since October 2025 (Platformer), its chief executive has written that AI will 'reduce our total corporate workforce', and Garman himself said in 2024 that most developers might not be coding within 24 months. Garman's claim that juniors are the most fluent with AI tools cuts against the essay's other evidence that novices who lean on AI understand less of what they build. On Beane: his own bomb-disposal example shows a technology that improved novice learning ('Trainees learn better than they did before robots'), so separation is a design outcome, not a law. His evidence is from robotics, where the novice is physically displaced; a junior engineer still has full access to the code and the tool. No critique of The Skill Code by another researcher was opened.
alternative_explanations: Employer branding. Both statements are cheap to make and flattering. Neither comes with a number that could be checked later, apart from Amazon's 11,000.
Base effects. 'Tripling' tells you nothing without the starting point. If graduate hiring had been cut hard in 2023 to 2025, tripling could simply restore an earlier level.
Definition. If IBM counts career changers and returners as entry-level, the tripling is not all new graduates.

Cost. Garman's first argument is that juniors are the least expensive staff. Hiring them alongside cuts to middle management is consistent with cheapening the workforce as much as with protecting a pipeline.
Selling the tool. Garman's remark is wrapped in a pitch for Kiro as a way to teach juniors good practice. A cloud vendor benefits if customers keep large engineering teams that consume its services.

Different jobs, same title. IBM's juniors now spend more time with clients and marketing. That may build commercial skill while reducing the time spent learning to read and reason about code, which is the skill the essay is worried about.
Beane's residents may have been failed by scheduling and supervision rules as much as by the robot. A hospital could have changed how console time was allocated.
verification_status: Checked against a source actually opened: LaMoreaux's Fortune quotes (Fortune article read in full); the Charter versions of the same quotes and the date and venue of the remarks (Charter article read in full); Krishna's CNN quote as reproduced by Fortune (CNN itself not opened); the date of the Berman video (YouTube page metadata, 18 August 2025); the wording and context of Garman's remark (YouTube auto-captions, which are machine-generated, so the exact words between 'like' and 'dumbest' are not certain); The Register's version (read in full); all WIRED quotes (read in full, dated 16 December 2025); the Platformer quotes and the 11,000 figure (read in full); the Beane TED quotes (official TED transcript); the ASQ abstract (Crossref); the HarperCollins description. Not checked against a primary source: anything said to be in the text of The Skill Code itself, since the book was not opened; the Bloomberg report credited with breaking the IBM story; the Axios detail on IBM's definition of entry-level and the US and 2026 scope; the Korn Ferry 37% figure; the 5.6% graduate unemployment figure; Beane's June 2024 opinion piece quoted by MIT Sloan. The Beane quotes from MIT Sloan are a journalist's transcription of a talk, not his published text.
relevance_to_essay: This is the leadership-response strand. Two large employers say out loud that cutting juniors empties the pipeline, which supports the essay's question about who will be senior in five years. Neither says how the juniors will be trained, beyond rewritten roles (IBM) and an AI tool that guides them (AWS). That gap is where the essay's proposal sits. Beane supplies the mechanism for why hiring alone is not enough: a senior with a capable tool has no practical reason to bring the junior into the work, so the learning has to be designed in.
implications_for_training_design: Nothing here tests a training format, so there is no evidence on frequency or on katas and treasure hunts. Beane's framework gives design criteria that can be quoted as his view, not as proven results. Challenge: exercises should sit near the edge of what the junior can do and feel uncomfortable, which argues against AI doing the hard part. Complexity: juniors need exposure to the wider system, which is a reasonable argument for a guided tour or hunt through the codebase. Connection: the expert has to be near. His bomb-disposal example worked because the senior sat beside the junior and talked through live work, so a challenge delivered by AI with no senior engineer reviewing or discussing it would miss the third C. Garman's Kiro point and Beane's 2018 call to 'build AI to help: to coach learners as they struggle' both allow AI a role in generating or guiding exercises. IBM's redesign moves juniors toward clients and marketing, which is a caution: a training programme needs to protect time on code comprehension specifically.
open_questions: How many entry-level people IBM hired before and after, and whether the tripling is US-only and includes non-graduates. Whether LaMoreaux said 'double down' or 'doubled down' (no recording opened). The exact words Garman spoke (the audio was not listened to) and which 'leadership group' he meant. What The Skill Code says in its own words, and whether it discusses software engineers at all. Whether either company has any data showing its juniors are learning the craft under the new arrangements.
